newsitem.title: UK: Full text of Jan UK purchasing managers' survey.
newsitem.headline: Full text of Jan UK purchasing managers' survey.

text.p: Following is the full text of the January Report on Business (Purchasing Managers' Survey) of the Chartered Institute of Purchasing and Supply (CIPS):
ORDERS, OUTPUT AND EMPLOYMENT GROWTH ACCELERATE WHILE STRONGER POUND LEADS TO FURTHER FALL IN INPUT PRICES.

The pace of UK manufacturing growth accelerated in January for the first time since last October. The Purchasing Managers' Index*, which provides an overall view of manufacturing activity, rose from 52.8 in December to 54.0, signalling growth for the eighth month running.

The improvement in the PMI was driven by an increase in the rate of growth of new orders. Rising domestic demand (especially for consumer goods) provided the main impetus behind the boost to order books. Export demand, although subdued compared with the summer, continued to show modest growth.

The overall rate of growth of output, having slipped over the previous three months, picked up in response to the strengthened order books. More inputs were bought than in December to meet these higher production requirements but, despite this increase in demand for supplies, the availability of inputs remained good. Less than 6.0 percent of panel members reported slower deliveries -- longer delivery times tend to be associated with capacity constraints.
OUTPUT

The seasonally adjusted rate of growth of output picked up in January, having decelerated over the previous three months. Production of consumer goods showed the largest rise followed by production of components. Both rose in reaction to increased demand. Output of investment goods, on the other hand, fell marginally for the first time in six months reflecting subdued capital expenditures by firms.
NEW ORDERS

The rate of growth of new orders accelerated in January. Order books have now risen for eight consecutive months with the latest survey again showing demand for consumer goods to have registered the greatest improvement. In spite of the strong pound, export orders rose on the whole during the month, although the rate of growth remains below that reported in the summer.
QUANTITY OF PURCHASES

The quantity of goods purchased for use in production rose in response to faster growth of output. However, the index remains subdued relative to both Output and New Orders Indexes due to the continued efforts made by panel members to keep stocks as low as possible in order to reduce costs.
PRICES

After seasonal adjustment for annual price reviews, the January Prices Index signalled the largest monthly fall in purchase prices since last August. Lower import prices, arising from the appreciation in the value of the pound over the past year, were widely reported by purchasing managers. Historically weak world-wide demand for many raw materials further helped panel members negotiate lower prices.
SUPPLIERS' DELIVERY TIMES

The seasonally adjusted Suppliers' Delivery Times Index remained below 50.0 in January, indicating a lengthening of delivery times for the fifth consecutive month. This lengthening reflected delays as certain suppliers were unable to expand output quickly enough to cope with rising demand levels. However, the incidence of such delays remained very low, with less than 6 percent of panel members reporting problems.
STOCKS OF PURCHASES

Stocks of purchases fell again in January as the drive to keep stocks at a minimum to cut costs continued (a process aided by good availability of cheap supplies). However, the seasonally adjusted Stocks of Purchases Index signalled the smallest decline in stocks since September last year, reflected some restocking following unusually severe stock reduction in December in advance of year-end stock-takes.

The absence of capacity constraints was generally linked to weak world-wide demand for many key raw materials, which also led to a softening of prices paid by panel members for inputs. However, by far the most significant factor affecting input prices was the exchange rate. The appreciation of sterling, as well as subduing export performance to a certain extent in recent months, again led to a sharp fall in many import prices. As a result, prices showed their sharpest drop since last August.

With the availability of cheap supplies remaining good, firms continued to focus upon keeping stocks as low as possible. Stocks of purchases fell sharply as a consequence, although by less than in December. Deliberate destocking policies were also commonly cited as a cause of the further fall in finished goods stock which occurred during the month. The fall in these stocks was not as marked as in December, however, due to a greater incidence of stock building in preparation for anticipated stronger demand in coming months.
Employment also rose in line with expectations of future growth. This, the sixth consecutive monthly rise in employment, was also the largest rise seen for nearly two years.

* The Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) is a composite indicator designed to provide an overall view of activity in the manufacturing economy and acts as a leading indicator for the whole economy. The indicator is derived from individual diffusion indices which measure changes in output, new orders, employment, suppliers' delivery times and stocks of goods purchased. A reading of the PMI below 50% indicates that the manufacturing economy is generally declining; above 50%, that it is generally expanding. The seasonally adjusted index may be subject to revision as improved estimation of seasonal adjustments occur with each month's new data.
STOCKS OF FINISHED GOODS

The combination of deliberate destocking policies, designed to cut costs, and an increased rate of dispatches to customers led to a further fall in finished goods inventories in January. Almost twice as many companies saw stocks fall than saw stocks rise. In almost all cases where stocks rose the increase was intentional to meet forecast growth in demand.
EMPLOYMENT

Seasonally adjusted employment rose for the sixth month in a row in January and also showed the largest monthly rise recorded since March 1995. The latest rise was largely confined to component manufacturers and producers of consumer goods and was intended to meet anticipated growth of orders. Producers of capital goods cut employment on the whole, reflecting greater pessimism in this sector.
CONSUMER GOODS

New orders for consumer goods showed the second largest monthly rise yet recorded by this survey (January 1993 saw the largest). Orders from UK customers saw the sharpest increase, but export orders also remained strong in spite of the strength of the pound. The rate of growth of output picked up sharply to meet the improvement in order books and stocks of purchases rose for the first time since June last year, reflecting widespread restocking to meet the greater activity.

Prices fell again and delivery times were largely unchanged on the previous month, indicating an absence of inflationary pressures. Employment, however, showed the slowest growth since last September as the incidence of job-shedding rose.
INVESTMENT/CAPITAL GOODS

Manufacturers of investment goods reported the weakest performance of the three Report on Business sectors in January. New orders increased again in January, but export demand showed only modest growth, attributed by panel members to the strength of sterling. Domestic demand also recorded slower growth compared with recent months. Output fell very marginally as a result -- the first fall since last August -- and employment was also trimmed in line with increased uncertainty regarding future business activity. Producers again stressed the need to keep stock levels as low as possible. The resulting weak demand for supplies, combined with the reduced price of imports, led to the sharpest fall in prices in this sector since the survey began.
INTERMEDIATE GOODS

Output of intermediate goods (components) strengthened again in January, the eighth consecutive monthly improvement. Export performance was reported to have been affected by the appreciation of sterling since the summer, but both total order levels and export orders were nevertheless higher than in the previous month. The acceleration in the rate of growth of output and orders led these intermediate goods producers to both increase employment and buy more goods than the other two market sectors. Suppliers again had to lengthen delivery times to meet this growing demand for inputs. Prices, however, fell sharply again due to the increased purchasing power of the stronger pound in foreign markets.
